hi All. I was coming to the group to write about my experience and suggest some thing to the package.
firstly, I should have read this before I start, but now my personal computer (iMac 2011 or 2012) is running in analysing more than 800 samples, each about 300 MB. I am having no problem rather than it is taking too long ( who worried about time if we are at home any way those days lol ) it has been almost two days now and still another two days are needed ( I think ).  I didn't want to run them in smaller splits thinking that the results would't be in a single CSV file.
I think the package is running smoothly, thanks to Vicncet and his team.

One suggestion, If it would be possible to calculate the time it need to process the data, it would be great. I remember reading about another package that can do that, but I can't remember the name.

One last thing, if anyone has materials about interpreting the results, please let me know.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I used this package to run the 7-day PA data.
The summary file report only shows the time in MVPA but no LPA, MPA, VPA, and sedentary time. I looked up the Part 5 summary file found the variables:

sleep duration = dur_nightsleep_min

sedentary time = dur_TINday_min

LPA time = dur_TLIGday_min

MPA time = dur_TMODday_min

VPA time = dur_TVIGday_min

Total wear time = dur_nightandday_min

Non-wear time = nonwear_hours

To me understanding, this should be the average daily LPA, MPA, VPA, MVPA. But it turns out there is a huge difference between the GGIR file report and the Part 5 variables. Can anyone help me with this issue? should I divide by 7 days for those variables?

Thanks!

Hi Laura,

Technically GGIR can handle data with a resolution as low as 3 Hertz, but from an interpretation perspective lower sample rates become more tricky. Follow the Nyquist-Shannon theorem a signal captures the frequencies below half its sample rate. So, a 10 Hertz recording captures frequencies below 5 Hertz. If you believe that frequencies above 5 hertz are either impossible or irrelevant for what you are trying to measure then no problem. However, if you have reason to believe otherwise then this could be an issue.
I guess is that magnitude of acceleration will be more strongly affected than sleep estimates. To be on the save side I generally recommend recording at higher sample rates.

Best,
Vincent

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] visualiation_sleep file
messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] visualiation_sleep file
messages.body_plain:
It looks like the participant id numbers were not succesfully extracted from the file names by which GGIR decided to use the file name as alternative file identifier. However, the visualisation is not designed to account for that.

Best solution is probably to either figure out how GGIR can extract the id number of your participants (argument idloc) or append the start of each filename with 12345_ where '12345' should be replaced by the id of the participant it belongs to. For the latter approach you will need to set idloc = 2 to make GGIR search for the id number in the filename preceding the first underscore.

Vincent

hrs.del.start = 0

part4_nightsummary has only 7 nights sleep (part4.jpg)
part5_daysummary_MM has only 7 days (part5.jpg)

I also tried running with strategy = 2 with the same error.

Config included as well.

Is anyone else seeing this error? Or, am I missing something obvious?

My goal is process a folder with multiple tests, but each test can be a different number of days.

Any help is much appreciated,

Matt

messages.subject_clean: [GGIR] Problem with data files longer than 7 days
messages.body_plain:
I think this is related to argument nnights, which by default in GGIR seems to be set at 7... Not good, we need to change this to c() such that the default setting is not to constrain the number of nights/days.

If you do nnights = c() or fill in the number of nights you expect in the data, it should process all of them.

Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

For a specific with study with workers, we are trying to estimate PA metrics (MVPA, ENMO, etc) during working and non-working hours.

However, there is huge variability in the working hours across our sample, even within participants. For example, one participant might have his/her shift from 8 am to 1 pm on Monday, from 10 am to 6:30 pm on Tuesday and so on…there is no standard at all.

It does not seem very logical, but I am considering to run GGIR using qwindow=c(seq(0,24,by=1)), generate a binary variable to classify each hour as a ‘working hour’ (yes/no) for each participant, and then collapse average of the PA metrics by participants and working x nonworking hours.

I wonder whether have anyone faced this issue when working with GGIR and would suggest an alternative approach.

Thanks in advance

Regards,

Gregore

Basically, they are coming up because we are doing a boolean test on an element that can be a vector sometimes. Note that this warning only relates to generating plots. Check to see that all of your data is processed properly.

I beleive that other users were getting a similar warning with the 'match_loc' variable due to the same issue.

Here is some more information on the warning we are getting -

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/14170778/interpreting-condition-has-length-1-warning-from-if-function

Matt

Hi Matt,
This is not good. Warnings are there for a reason and this could lead to unpredictable behavior.

If wake_loc has a length longer than 1 than testing whether it equals 0 means that it tests whether every element in the vector equals zero and returns a new vector of those results.
R does this intentionally because testing every element in a vector is a useful element. To avoid this, always first test whether the length is 1 and then whether the value is 0, or change the test such that it does:
wake_loc == rep(0,length(wake_loc) in case you are interested to know whether all elements of wake_loc are zero.

Can you correct this?
Thanks, Vincent
